nameStory: The 'trailing' part of this plant's name comes from its habit of sprawling along the ground rather than standing upright. It's called a 'snapdragon' because its tubular flowers have a hinged lower lip that snaps shut when squeezed, just like the familiar garden snapdragons we know and love.
description: Trailing snapdragon is a low-growing, sprawling perennial that hugs the ground with soft, fuzzy stems. This charming little plant produces small snapdragon-like flowers that are typically pale yellow or cream-colored. It rarely grows more than a few inches tall but can spread outward to form small mats. Originally from France and Spain, it's an uncommon sight in New England gardens and naturalized areas.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small, tubular snapdragon-type flowers with two lips - an upper hood and a lower lip that closes when gently squeezed, usually pale yellow or creamy white

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Sprawling, mat-forming plant that trails along the ground rather than growing upright, with soft, somewhat sticky stems

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Small, heart-shaped to rounded leaves that feel soft and slightly fuzzy or sticky to the touch, arranged alternately along the trailing stems

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Entire plant has a soft, downy feel with tiny hairs that may make stems and leaves slightly sticky when handled

habitat: In New England, trailing snapdragon is extremely rare and typically found only in cultivated settings like rock gardens or as an escaped garden plant. When it does naturalize, it prefers well-drained, sandy or rocky soils in sunny to partially shaded locations. It may occasionally be found growing in cracks in stone walls or similar disturbed areas with good drainage.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as soft, trailing stems begin to spread. Early flowers may appear in late spring in protected locations.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming period when the small snapdragon flowers are most abundant and easily spotted against the green foliage mat.
seasonality.fall: Plants may continue blooming into early fall in mild weather, with stems becoming more woody and established.
seasonality.winter: In harsh New England winters, plants typically die back significantly or completely, surviving as roots in protected locations.

funFact: Despite being called a snapdragon, trailing snapdragon was recently moved out of the traditional snapdragon family (Scrophulariaceae) and into the plantain family - making it a closer relative to common lawn plantain than to garden snapdragons!
confusionNotes: With only 2 recorded observations in New England, trailing snapdragon is so rare that confusion with other plants is unlikely. If encountered, it might be mistaken for other small, trailing plants with tubular flowers, but the distinctive snapdragon flower shape that closes when squeezed is the key identifying feature.
contextualKnowledge: Many plants once called 'snapdragons' in North America have been reclassified into different genera entirely. True Asarina snapdragons are now considered exclusively Old World plants, while most of the climbing or trailing snapdragons you might find in American gardens belong to related but separate genera like Maurandya or Lophospermum.
compareHints: Trailing snapdragon is the only member of its genus, so comparison within Asarina isn't possible. Within the plantain family, it's quite different from most relatives - while common plantains have tiny, inconspicuous flowers in spikes, trailing snapdragon has showy, snapdragon-like blooms. Its trailing habit and tubular flowers make it unique among New England members of the plantain family.
